title: The past sentence that flips everything
goal: Mastering the one truly hard rule in Pashto: in a past sentence with an object, the doer moves into the oblique form and the verb agrees with the OBJECT, not the doer.
bekal: make past sentences with verbs that take an object
move the doer into the oblique form: ما، تا، هغه، هغې
match the verb to the gender and number of its object

dialogs.title: خبرې اترې — پرون مې څه وکړل
dialogs.intro: Ahmad finds Budi on the veranda with a notebook full of scribbles. One rule is refusing to sink in.

lines.speaker: احمد:
lines.id: Budi, what are you writing? You look tired.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: زه تېر مهال زده کوم. خو یو څه نه پوهېږم.
lines.baca: zə ter mahāl zdə kawəm. kho yaw tsə nə poheẓəm.
lines.id: I'm studying the past tense. But there's one thing I don't understand.
lines.literal: I past time study do-I. but one thing not understand-I.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: زه پرون ولاړم — دا روښانه ده. خو زه پرون کتاب ولوستم؟
lines.baca: zə parūn wlāṛəm — dā roṣāna da. kho zə parūn kitāb wə́lwastəm?
lines.id: زه پرون ولاړم — that's clear. But "yesterday I read a book"?
lines.literal: I yesterday went-I — this clear is. but I yesterday book read-I?

lines.speaker: احمد:
lines.text: نه. هلته زه نه وایې، ما وایې. ما کتاب ولوست.
lines.baca: nə. halta zə nə waye, mā waye. mā kitāb wə́lwast.
lines.id: No. There you don't say زه, you say ما. ما کتاب ولوست.
lines.literal: no. there I not say-you, me-OBL say-you. me-OBL book read-PAST.

lines.speaker: احمد:
lines.text: ځکه چې فعل کتاب پسې ځي، نه ما پسې.
lines.baca: dzəka che fi'l kitāb pase dzī, nə mā pase.
lines.id: Because the verb follows کتاب, not ما.
lines.literal: because that verb book after goes, not me-OBL after.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: So what if the object is ډوډۍ?

lines.speaker: احمد:
lines.text: ډوډۍ ښځینه ده، نو ما ډوډۍ وخوړه.
lines.baca: ḍoḍəy ṣədzīna da, no mā ḍoḍəy wə́khoṛa.
lines.id: ډوډۍ is feminine, so ما ډوډۍ وخوړه.
lines.literal: bread feminine is, so me-OBL bread ate-FEM.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: And if there are lots of books?

lines.speaker: احمد:
lines.text: ما کتابونه ولوستل. جمع، نو فعل هم جمع.
lines.baca: mā kitābūna wə́lwastəl. jam', no fi'l ham jam'.
lines.id: ما کتابونه ولوستل. The object is plural, so the verb is plural too.
lines.literal: me-OBL books read-PL. plural, so verb also plural.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: نو په تېر مهال کې فعل زه نه ګوري؟
lines.baca: no pə ter mahāl ke fi'l zə nə gorī?
lines.id: So in the past, the verb doesn't see "I" at all?
lines.literal: so in past time in verb me not see-it?

lines.speaker: احمد:
lines.text: سمه ده. خو یوازې کله چې مفعول وي.
lines.baca: sama da. kho yawāze kəla che maf'ūl wī.
lines.id: Right. But only when there's an object.
lines.literal: right is. but only when that object is.

lines.speaker: احمد:
lines.text: هېڅ نه بدلېږي. زه کتاب لولم. عادي جمله ده.
lines.baca: hets nə badleẓī. zə kitāb lwaləm. 'ādī jumla da.
lines.id: No change at all. زه کتاب لولم. A normal sentence.
lines.literal: at-all not changes. I book read-I. normal sentence is.

notes: 🔴 This is the single most important rule in the whole module, and the only one with no counterpart at all in English. Read the grammar box twice, then go back to the dialogue and trace every line.

Note that there are **two** conditions, and both must hold at once: the sentence must be **past**, and the verb must **have an object**. If either is missing, everything is normal. Present sentences are always normal; past sentences without an object you already learned in unit 12.

The oblique form of the doer is nothing new. You already used it in unit 6 with prepositions: ما ته (to me), تا سره (with you). The exact same forms now work as the doer of a past sentence, and that's why unit 6 came first.

⚠️ The most common beginner mistake isn't using the wrong oblique form but **forgetting to change the verb**. ما کتاب ولوستم sounds wrong to Afghans, because the ـم at the end points to "I", while a past verb with an object must never point to its doer.
A check that never fails: ask yourself "what was done?". If there's an answer, that's the object, and your verb must agree with it. If there's no answer, the verb agrees with the doer as usual.

Linguists have a name for this rule: split ergativity. Pashto shares it with Urdu, Hindi, Kurdish, and Basque — but not with Persian, even though the two are neighbors. You don't need the term; you just need to be able to use it.

grammars.title: 🔴 The whole rule in three lines
body: Line one: **present** sentences are always normal. The doer is in the usual form, and the verb agrees with the doer. Example: زه کتاب لولم.
Line two: **past sentences without an object** are also normal. The doer is in the usual form, and the verb agrees with the doer. Example: زه ولاړم.
Line three: **past sentences with an object** flip everything. The doer goes into the **oblique** form, and the verb agrees with the **object** — its gender and number. Example: ما کتاب ولوست.

grammars.title: The oblique doer, and four verb endings
body: The left column shows the doer forms you must use in a past sentence with an object. Note that only زه، ته، and هغه (feminine) really change; the rest just happen to stay the same.
The right column shows the verb endings, and they're far simpler than you'd expect: only **four** options, decided entirely by the object. There's no form for "I", "you", or "we" at all.

sections.title: Drilling the rule until it's automatic

blocks.text: This rule won't stick through explanation; it sticks through repeating whole sentences. The ten lines below are the sentences you'll need most, and all of them use the same rule. Read them out loud, then cover the Pashto column.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Line eight, and why it's so strange
items: The sentence تا زه ولیدم means "you saw me", and the verb ends in ـم. That ending doesn't point to "you" but to **زه**, which here is the object.
This is the starkest proof that a past verb with an object really is blind to its doer. All it sees is the thing acted on, even when that thing happens to be a person.
Compare this pair until you feel it: ما ته ولیدې (I saw you) and تا زه ولیدم (you saw me). The doers swap, but what decides the verb ending is still the object.
If this feels like your head is upside down, that's normal. Give it three days, do this unit's exercises twice, and don't move on until all ten sentences in the table above come out without thinking.

blocks.text: Past forms of the ten most common verbs with an object

blocks.title: If you can only memorize one thing
items: Memorize **ما** as the word that opens a story about the past. As soon as you start telling what you did yesterday, the sentence almost always opens with ما, not زه.
If you're unsure, you can leave the verb in the masculine singular. ما ډوډۍ وخوړ isn't perfect, but it's far better than ما ډوډۍ وخوړم — the latter sounds wrong, the former just sounds foreign.
⚠️ Don't mix the two forms. زه کتاب ولوستم is the most glaring mistake, because it uses the normal doer **and** a doer ending at the same time.
Listen to Afghans telling stories. Within a week your ear will notice that stories about the past almost always open with ما، تا، هغه، مونږ — and that's a quicker cue than any table.

exercises.prompt: Choose the right doer: زه or ما.
Choose the right past verb form for the object. The base form is in brackets.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: ما ډوډۍ وخوړه. — ما هغه ولید. — تا څه وویل؟ — هغې لیک ولیکه. — مونږ کار وکړ.
ما کتاب ولوست. — ما ډوډۍ وخوړه. — تا څه وویل؟ — هغې لیک ولیکه. — مونږ کار وکړ.
wave: For the next three days, start every story about yesterday with ما. If your sentence comes out with زه and a verb ending in ـم in a sentence with an object, stop and start over — three correct repetitions are worth more than twenty wrong sentences.
